newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish fundamentals sound despite flood - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Polish fundamentals sound despite flood - IMF.

text.p: Poland's fundamentals are sound despite flood damage, but domestic demand should be curbed to prevent the widening current account gap from slipping out of control, the International Monetary Fund's representative said on Wednesday.

"Although the present level of the current account deficit (4-5 percent of GDP in 1997) is not a problem, a further significant deterioration would make Poland vulnerable to sudden shifts in confidence and resulting economic and financial disruptions," Markus Rodlauer told a news conference.
"To stabilise the current account deficit at a susainable level, the expansion of domestic demand...currently growing much faster than output, should slow significantly," he said.
Rodlauer said Poland should significantly reduce next year's budget gap from this year's planned 2.8 percent of gross domestic product deficit and balance the budget thereafter.
"At a minimum the fiscal deficit should be reduced to 1.5 percent in 1998 and eliminated later," he said.
He said fiscal tightening should be combined with monetary tightening.

"Monetary policy should contain the rapid growth of bank credits which has accommodated the recent surge in domestic demand. Growing wage pressures, especially in the state sector, need to be checked," he added.
Rodlauer said that he was not worried by the the recent zloty weakening and its higher volatility within the 14-percent trading band would help Poland limit pressures from short-term capital inflows.
"A somewhat greater use of the fluctuation bands would help contain the pressures from capital flows," he said.
He said a weaker and more unpredictable zloty had created room for monetary tightening and higher interest rates in particular.

"The fact that the zloty has trended down somewhat within the band with more fluctuations than in the past is not of particular concern and actually indicates that there is now scope for the tightening of the monetary policy," he said.
Rodlauer said that despite damage inflicted by two weeks of heavy flooding in southern Poland the country's overall economic fundamentals appeared not to have deteriorated.
"Have the floods worsened the fundamentals of Poland? While it is too early for precise estimates of the physical damage and costs, my assesment at this point is 'no'," he said.
Rodlauer said that the floods would have little direct impact on Poland's current account deficit providing financial discipline and stability were not relaxed.
